brief.head: Medium foolish
brief.text: Promoters who siphon off cash can do it a cou­ple of times, Ajay Shah said, be­fore lenders wise up. India’s credit mar­kets are “medium fool­ish”, not deeply fool­ish. {080-J06}

brief.head: A suspect word
brief.text: “The word stake­holder is a sure sign of fee­ble rea­son­ing,” Ajay Shah said. Whether to sell or break up a failed firm is a cold busi­ness call. {080-C04}

brief.head: Banks prefer the dark
brief.text: Banks, Ajay Shah said, like to ne­go­ti­ate in dark­ness, one cred­i­tor at a time, rather than be­fore the full com­mit­tee. Amit Varma’s reply: sun­light is the best dis­in­fec­tant[[x4]]. {080-J18}

brief.head: A virtuous cycle
brief.text: India’s re­forms of 1991 to 2011 worked, Ajay Shah said, be­cause cap­i­tal con­trols, the eq­uity mar­ket, soft­ware and tele­com were being fixed in par­al­lel, each strength­en­ing the oth­ers. {080-C15}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how firms should die
lead.head: Let dead firms lie

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 80

body: Amit Varma began by declar­ing that firms are awe­some, amaz­ing, ed­i­fy­ing and il­lu­mi­nat­ing. Ajay Shah had come to talk about how they die.
The econ­o­mist Joseph Schumpeter’s cre­ative de­struc­tion, Shah said, needs both birth and death: “You need the cre­ation of firms, you need Vishnu, and you need Shiv.” {080-C01}
When an old firm fails, he said, its labour and cap­i­tal are not lost. They flow back to other firms, as a body’s atoms re­turn to other forms of life.
What fol­lowed was Shah’s mas­ter­class on how bank­ruptcy should work, and how it has worked in India, where he sat on the com­mit­tee that shaped the law.
## The day of de­fault
A com­pany, Shah said, is run by its share­hold­ers only while they pay their dues. The day they de­fault, they are thrown out, and the cred­i­tors take con­trol. {080-C03}
A judge has two ques­tions to set­tle, and only two: was there credit, and was there a de­fault?
After that, speed is ev­ery­thing. A fail­ing firm is “a melt­ing ice cube”[[x1]], Shah said: key em­ploy­ees leave, sup­pli­ers hold back goods, ma­chines go un­main­tained. {080-C06}
Delay has an­other cost. A firm propped up with fresh loans be­comes a zom­bie, eat­ing the mar­gins of healthy ri­vals. Japan, Shah said, lost thirty years this way.
Once in charge, cred­i­tors must de­cide whether the firm is worth more kept run­ning or bro­ken up. That, Shah in­sisted, is a busi­ness judg­ment, not a hu­man­i­tar­ian one.
Their forum is the com­mit­tee of cred­i­tors, where clash­ing claims are hag­gled over. What India needs, he said, is “a badass com­mer­cially so­phis­ti­cated com­mit­tee of cred­i­tors”. {080-C08}
## A C-grade code
India’s Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code be­came law in 2016. Shah’s ver­dict on the re­form he helped bring about was blunt: “it is a B grade or a C grade project so far.”
Varma protested that the work of Shah, Susan Thomas and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah was being dis­missed “by some ran­dom uncle as third rate”.

The trou­ble starts with the banks. Their over­rid­ing ob­jec­tive, Shah said, is “how to hide the bad news”: they delay, and worry more about a fu­ture CBI in­ves­ti­ga­tion than about re­cov­er­ing money.

The NCLT works like any other Indian court. The new reg­u­la­tor was built from eight sec­tions pasted out of the SEBI Act. And pro­mot­ers, barred from bid­ding for their own firms, qui­etly re­struc­ture loans with banks in se­cret.
## In the shadow of the law
The real test, Shah ar­gued, is the out­come: a credit mar­ket where bor­row­ers are keen to repay and lenders keen to lend.

Few cases should need a court. “In ad­vanced economies, most trans­ac­tions are pri­vately ne­go­ti­ated be­tween the cred­i­tors and the share­hold­ers under the threat of the law,” he said. {080-C12}

Varma called “in the shadow of the law” the key phrase of the episode. The law, he ar­gued, is more than a statute: it in­cludes state ca­pa­bil­ity and the ex­pec­ta­tion of en­force­ment. “Unless all of that is in place, just writ­ing a great law doesn’t make sense.”

Above all, Shah said, a re­form needs re­searchers and crit­ics to keep it hon­est. India pro­duces per­haps two pa­pers a year on bank­ruptcy where twenty are needed. Without that pipe­line, “noth­ing will ever get fixed”.

second.label: The regulator
second.head: Cut, paste, malfunction
second.deck: How 140 sections for a new regulator gave way to eight from SEBI

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the regulator that was cut and pasted

body: The orig­i­nal draft of India’s bank­ruptcy law had about 140 sec­tions on how to build[[x2]] its new reg­u­la­tor, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India[[x3]]: checks and bal­ances, sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers, gov­er­nance, Ajay Shah said. {080-S05}
All of it was deleted. Instead, some­one cut and pasted some eight sec­tions from the SEBI Act into the IBBI, and SEBI’s mal­func­tions came with them.

The IBBI then hit the lim­its of Indian state ca­pa­bil­ity on day one, along with the pull every gov­ern­ment agency feels to­wards more power. In a British com­mon law sys­tem, Shah added, such rules would evolve as mar­ket prac­tice. India waits for the reg­u­la­tor to write them. {080-C11}

quote.text: So all the bad prac­tices of how SEBI mal­func­tions were brought into IBBI.

third.head: A rat trap under the chair
body: In India, the pro­moter of a bank­rupt firm can­not even bid to buy it back. In prin­ci­ple, Ajay Shah said, that is a mis­take: pro­mot­ers know the busi­ness best and would prob­a­bly bid higher.

But he ac­cepts the counter-argument. A pro­moter ex­pect­ing to re­turn could leave poi­son pills: “messy things in­side the com­pany that she knows about, that she un­der­stands, that she will be able to defuse once she is back in charge”. {080-C10}
Amit Varma pic­tured “a rat trap in the cor­ner of­fice under the chair under the table”. “That’s lit­er­ally what can be done,” Shah replied. {080-J09}
With weak rule of law, he said, such traps go un­pun­ished. So India has two bad ex­tremes: pro­mot­ers shut out of for­mal bank­ruptcy, and banks qui­etly re­struc­tur­ing their loans in se­cret.

box.title: The idea behind the episode
box.text: The econ­o­mist Joseph Schumpeter tied progress to the birth and death of firms. Innovators earn a tem­po­rary mo­nop­oly rent on new ideas; old firms that can­not keep up go bank­rupt. Creative de­struc­tion, Ajay Shah said, re­quires both. {080-C01}

sections.label: First principles
sections.head: Vishnu builds, Shiva clears
sections.caption: creative destruction
body: Creative de­struc­tion, Ajay Shah said, needs birth and death alike: Vishnu and Shiva. Without both, he said, “the har­mony of the world is in­com­plete.” {080-C01}

Firms take labour and cap­i­tal and or­gan­ise them in par­tic­u­lar ways, he said, much as an organism’s DNA holds the recipe for as­sem­bling atoms and mol­e­cules. It is easy to grow emo­tional about ei­ther. But the recipe may be a bad one, or the world may move on.

In the econ­o­mist Joseph Schumpeter’s story of progress, in­no­va­tors take risks and earn a tem­po­rary mo­nop­oly on a new idea, and the prospect of that rent drives re­search. Old firms that can­not keep up go bank­rupt, and their labour and cap­i­tal pass to other firms.
## Adapt or make way

Amit Varma of­fered two ax­ioms: the world is com­plex, and the world is in flux. {080-C02} So people’s needs can­not be met by cen­tral plan­ning, only from the bot­tom up, through the price sys­tem Friedrich Hayek de­scribed.

Firms that meet needs earn prof­its. Adaptation, Varma said, “is learn­ing how to keep serv­ing other peo­ple in so­ci­ety”, and a firm that fails to adapt should go out of busi­ness so its labour and re­sources can be bet­ter used.
~ Some firms do adapt. The Tata Steel of 2024, Shah said, is un­recog­nis­ably dif­fer­ent from Jamsetji Tata’s. Many oth­ers will not man­age it, and should go out of busi­ness. {080-J14}

quote.text: One of them is that the world is com­plex, and the other one is that the world is in flux.

sections.label: The firm
sections.head: When creditors take the keys
sections.caption: what happens on default
body: A firm starts with cap­i­tal from its share­hold­ers and usu­ally bor­rows too, Ajay Shah said. Borrowing need not mean a bank loan: rent cam­era equip­ment for a show and pay later, and the owner is your cred­i­tor. Operational and fi­nan­cial cred­i­tors are both cred­i­tors.

As the com­pany was con­ceived in Europe in the 15th and 16th cen­turies, the share­hold­ers make every de­ci­sion as long as they ser­vice their debts. The cred­i­tor has no say, only a claim: pay in 100 ru­pees, ex­pect 110 after a year. {#interest}
## A new bal­ance sheet

When the firm fails to pay, a cred­i­tor goes be­fore a judge, who need es­tab­lish only that there was credit and a de­fault. Then the share­hold­ers lose con­trol and, usu­ally, their cap­i­tal too. {080-C03}

Take a com­pany with 100 ru­pees of eq­uity and 100 of debt that de­faults. It is re­built on a brand new bal­ance sheet, with the eq­uity hold­ers gone and the cred­i­tors in con­trol. “It is that deep,” Shah said.

~ Too many Indians, he lamented, miss these ba­sics and grow sen­ti­men­tal about a com­pany, its old share­hold­ers and its found­ing fam­ily. In 15th- and 16th-century England, he said, there was no sen­ti­men­tal­ism around such things.

quote.text: The day the share­hold­ers fail to pay their dues, they’re sup­posed to get thrown out and re­placed by the cred­i­tors.

sections.label: The case for speed
sections.head: Propped up, dragging down
sections.caption: zombie firms and melting ice cubes
body: Suppose a weak firm is propped up with more and more debt, Ajay Shah said, be­cause badly reg­u­lated banks will not admit the prob­lem or the gov­ern­ment is prod­ding them. It keeps com­pet­ing with healthy firms and dam­ag­ing their profit mar­gins.
“These firms that are dead men walk­ing are called zom­bie firms,” he said. Banks in the same state are zom­bie banks. {080-C05}
Without prof­its, healthy firms do not in­vest. A kept-alive Air India[[x8]] or Jet Airways, Shah said, drives down fares and harms qual­ity air­lines like Vistara. {#vistara}
## The ice cube
Delay also helps the guilty. A pro­moter fam­ily al­ways knows more than out­siders, Shah said, and when it sees trou­ble com­ing it may start steal­ing cash. Every week of delay gives it more time.

Meanwhile the firm falls apart: key em­ploy­ees leave, sup­pli­ers hold back goods, main­te­nance is skipped. “Once a firm starts get­ting into trou­ble, it’s a melt­ing ice cube[[x7]],” he said. {080-C06}

~ What every healthy so­ci­ety needs, Shah ar­gued, is an ob­jec­tive early warn­ing that sets the bank­ruptcy process going fast. Business fail­ure is nor­mal, he said, and should carry no stigma. {#stigma}

quote.text: Japan went through thirty years of mis­ery be­cause they had zom­bie banks which were keep­ing zom­bie firms aloft.

sections.label: The bargaining table
sections.head: Haggling, with a supermajority
sections.caption: the committee of creditors
body: Caught early, a fail­ing firm is worth more as a going con­cern than bro­ken up, Ajay Shah said. Its peo­ple, pro­cesses, IT sys­tems, cul­ture and out­side re­la­tion­ships add up to in­tan­gi­ble cap­i­tal, often worth a lot. Caught late, only liq­ui­da­tion is left. {080-C07}
Choosing be­tween them is a busi­ness judg­ment, not a hu­man­i­tar­ian one, Shah said; his ex­am­ple set 40 from liq­ui­da­tion against 70 from a sale as a going con­cern. {#forty}
## Who holds the fac­tory

Creditors’ in­ter­ests clash. A se­cured lender hold­ing the key fac­tory can threaten to tor­pedo a going-concern plan un­less it is paid first: “I want my hun­dred and you guys fig­ure out what­ever else you want to do.”
Decisions need a su­per­ma­jor­ity, not just 51 per cent but per­haps 60 or 70. {#supermajority}
Doing this well takes so­phis­ti­cated bar­gain­ing, Shah said, which rarely hap­pens in India be­cause most fi­nan­cial firms are “reg­u­lated to death” and run as bu­reau­cra­cies. {080-C08}

~ Many good bids are not all cash but prom­ises to repay over years. Judging whether to trust the bid­der can­not be re­duced to open­ing bids like gov­ern­ment pro­cure­ment, though that, Shah said, has been India’s in­stinct.

quote.text: If you get there soon enough, ac­tu­ally the value of the firm as a going con­cern is higher than the sum of the parts.

sections.label: The real world
sections.head: Hiding the bad news
sections.caption: why banks drag their feet
body: India has a bank­ruptcy process now, and it is bet­ter to have it than not, Ajay Shah said. But it is not a great one. {#cgrade}

The first prob­lem is the banks. By the time of bank­ruptcy, Shah said, the loss has al­ready hap­pened[[x9]]; the only ques­tion is who bears it. Yet banks carry the loan at full value and want to delay recog­nis­ing the loss. {080-C09}
Amit Varma de­scribed ev­er­green­ing: the bank lends the bor­rower fresh money to repay the old loan, and the can is kicked down the road.
## Painting the tape

Put such banks on a com­mit­tee of cred­i­tors and they will pro­pose an­other meet­ing next month, Shah said, while the firm melts. Public sec­tor and pri­vate bankers alike think of the CBI, and of whether a fu­ture in­ves­ti­ga­tion will find fault. {#cbi}

“That’s dif­fer­ent from a com­mer­cial in­stinct,”[[x10]] he said. His un­ortho­dox fix, which he ad­mit­ted would be hard to sell: until bank­ing reg­u­la­tion gets its act to­gether, cut the vot­ing power of banks in the com­mit­tee, since mu­tual funds, for­eign in­vestors, NBFCs and in­sur­ers are more com­mer­cial.

~ Varma wor­ried that bankers would not know the first thing about a bank­rupt bis­cuit fac­tory. Shah dis­agreed: they lent it a hun­dred crore ru­pees, so “they’re bloody well going to un­der­stand your in­dus­try”. {080-J07}

quote.text: So a core in­sight in bank­ruptcy is a busi­ness has failed, the loss has al­ready taken place.

sections.label: The way forward
sections.head: Living in the law’s shadow
sections.caption: the shadow of the law
body: Public pol­icy, Ajay Shah said, can be judged by its in­puts, out­puts and out­comes. In bank­ruptcy, the in­puts are the law, the NCLT and the com­mit­tees; the out­puts are cases and the money cred­i­tors get back.

The out­come that mat­ters is a work­ing credit mar­ket. Leverage in India, he said, should go up when a bank­ruptcy code comes in, and most dis­putes should be re­solved by pri­vate ne­go­ti­a­tion, “in the shadow of the law”. {080-C12}

For Amit Varma, the law in that phrase is more than a statute on paper. It is the in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture of state ca­pa­bil­ity[[x11]] and en­force­ment, and when that is bro­ken, the dam­age is “tur­tles all the way down”. {080-J19}
## Strong law, weak ground

A good law in a vac­uum, Varma ar­gued, means noth­ing. {080-C13} Shah framed it as a trade-off: pass a good law that per­forms weakly today and im­proves as other pieces fall into place, or set­tle for a weaker com­pro­mise suited to present con­di­tions.

~ Either way, Shah said, pass­ing the law and in­au­gu­rat­ing the reg­u­la­tor is only the be­gin­ning. Then starts “a process of it­er­a­tive re­fine­ment”, with data and re­searchers keep­ing the re­form hon­est.

quote.text: there is noth­ing called a good law or a good pol­icy in a vac­uum.
And I think most peo­ple in India don’t un­der­stand the im­por­tance of the knowl­edge ecosys­tem. That every area of work has to be en­sconced in a suc­cess­ful knowl­edge ecosys­tem.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: How India got its bankruptcy code, and the zombies it was meant to bury

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah retells KP Krishnan’s story of the code
stories.head: The paragraph that grew a code
body: In 2015, part A of the bud­get speech car­ried a para­graph from the Ministry of Small and Medium Enterprises, promis­ing a bank­ruptcy code for small com­pa­nies. {080-S03}

KP Krishnan took that para­graph to Jaitley, the fi­nance min­is­ter, Ajay Shah said, retelling a story Krishnan had told on *The Seen and the Unseen*. They could do that, Krishnan said, but could they not do big­ger, with a full bank­ruptcy code?
Jaitley’s ques­tion was prac­ti­cal: “Do we have the abil­ity? Do we have the teams?”

Krishnan pointed to the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission[[x12]], led by Justice Srikrishna from 2011 to 2015, which had shown that India could run large re­search teams and draft big, com­plex laws to a world-class stan­dard. {#fslrc}
So a com­mit­tee called the BLRC was set up, led by TK Viswanathan, a wise old hand from the world of the law min­istry. Shah and Susan Thomas were among its mem­bers.

Even then, it began with a nar­row plan: a few amend­ments to the Companies Act’s wind­ing-up pro­vi­sions. It took a while for peo­ple to see that a bank­ruptcy code plays at a dif­fer­ent level, as a ne­go­ti­a­tion mech­a­nism for cred­i­tors.
Rajiv Mehrishi, who be­came sec­re­tary of the Department of Economic Affairs, backed the more rad­i­cal view: not “dinky triv­ial re­fine­ments” but a full code.
~ Susan Thomas led the team that wrote the first draft, which be­came law in 2016 as the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
stories.why: Big re­form needs an am­bi­tious ask and a be­liev­able an­swer to whether it can be done. Here the an­swer came from ca­pa­bil­ity the FSLRC had built ear­lier, and even then a nar­row vi­sion had to be over­come.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma, who dis­cussed the draft­ing with Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah of Susan Thomas’s team, calls the in­side story “ab­so­lutely in­spir­ing”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on how a budget paragraph grew into a law

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Companies Act of 2013
stories.head: The chapters that never came
body: When India was writ­ing its new Companies Act of 2013, Ajay Shah said, Montek Singh Ahluwalia, deputy chair­man of the Planning Commission, told the Ministry of Company Affairs it should con­tain chap­ters form­ing a full bank­ruptcy code[[x13]], with col­lec­tive ne­go­ti­a­tion among cred­i­tors. {#chapters}
He was as­sured it would be done. It was not.
When Shah later raised the issue, Montek asked whether he was sure the code was not in the Act. Shah was. “I have done my fair share of bed­time read­ing of the Companies Act,” he said. {080-S02}
~ There were some triv­ial wind­ing-up pro­vi­sions, he said, but no bank­ruptcy process. It took a long time for peo­ple to un­der­stand such ba­sics.
stories.why: A prom­ise made in a min­istry is not law on paper. A real bank­ruptcy code is a ne­go­ti­a­tion mech­a­nism for cred­i­tors, quite un­like wind­ing-up clauses, and it took some­one who had ac­tu­ally read the statute to say so.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the bankruptcy code that never was

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on what zombies cost Japan
stories.head: A thirty-year hangover
body: After 1986[[x14]], Ajay Shah said, Japan’s Ministry of Finance and MITI[[x15]] ran an in­dus­trial pol­icy that kept bad firms ar­ti­fi­cially alive, propped up by bad banks. {080-S04}

The zom­bie firms kept com­pet­ing with healthy ones. “The pres­ence of these zom­bies shat­ters prof­itabil­ity for ev­ery­body else,” Shah said, so eco­nomic dy­namism drained away across the coun­try. {#shatters}
The cost, he said, ran to thirty years, and the whole thing went badly wrong. Healthy firms need prof­its in order to in­vest, and zom­bies take those prof­its away.

~ Amit Varma noted that Japan also made a lot of great zom­bie movies, and won­dered whether to go back and watch them with new eyes, for metaphors be­neath the sur­face: “dead man walk­ing, axe in hand, hand chopped off”. {080-J04}
stories.why: Keeping dead firms alive is not kind­ness, on Shah’s ac­count. It drains the prof­its that healthy firms need in order to in­vest, and as Japan found, the bill can run for decades.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Japan’s zombie banks

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a committee that took offence
stories.head: Not rude, just technical
body: Long ago, Ajay Shah said, he sat on the Percy Mistry com­mit­tee[[x16]] on Bombay as an in­ter­na­tional fi­nan­cial cen­tre.
There he and Mistry kept using the term “zom­bie bank”, and some mem­bers took of­fence, think­ing it a dis­re­spect­ful word. {080-S01}
But it is a tech­ni­cal word, Shah said. Zombie firms and zom­bie banks are terms that came out of the re­search on Japan, for in­sti­tu­tions that are dead men walk­ing.

~ Amit Varma, who had just been mus­ing on Japan’s zom­bie movies, ad­mit­ted that his own mem­ory was “pretty close to being a zom­bie”. {#memory} He thought the very first episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* was on zom­bie banks, and urged lis­ten­ers to look it up.

quote.text: And there Percy and I were mer­rily bandy­ing the word zom­bie bank around. And some peo­ple in the com­mit­tee got very of­fended.

quiz.q: Which two gods did Ajay Shah say Schumpeterian creative destruction needs?
quiz.a: Vishnu for the cre­ation of firms, and Shiva for their de­struc­tion.

quiz.q: What two questions alone should a judge ask when a creditor alleges default?
quiz.a: Whether there was a credit re­la­tion­ship, and whether there was in­deed a de­fault.

quiz.q: How long did Japan suffer from zombie banks keeping zombie firms aloft, by Shah’s account?
quiz.a: Thirty years of mis­ery, in the bad years after 1986.

quiz.q: What replaced the 140 sections drafted to build India’s new bankruptcy regulator, the IBBI?
quiz.a: Some eight sec­tions cut and pasted from the SEBI Act, mal­func­tions and all.

quiz.q: Why does Shah want to cut the voting power of banks on committees of creditors?
quiz.a: Banks hide losses and fear fu­ture CBI probes; other cred­i­tors are more com­mer­cial.

quiz.q: What is a poison pill in the bankruptcy of a promoter-run firm?
quiz.a: A hid­den trap the pro­moter leaves, which only she knows how to defuse.

A firm sold whole and kept run­ning, rather than bro­ken up.
A sup­plier owed money for goods or ser­vices given on credit.
A vote share above a sim­ple ma­jor­ity, such as 60 per cent.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 80. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0); Joseph Schumpeter (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Lawrence Lessig (Joi Ito, CC BY 2.0); Ronald Coase (University of Chicago Law School, Attribution). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Open Library and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Foundational bankruptcy and credit-risk research (papers at ifrogs.org and XKDR Forum’s firms-finance work)
shelf.why: The re­search base be­hind the Indian bank­ruptcy re­form.

shelf.title: Edited volume of papers on the Indian bankruptcy reform
shelf.creator: Susan Thomas (editor)
shelf.why: A col­lec­tion of se­ri­ous re­search on how the re­form was de­signed and how it has worked, which is the kind of knowl­edge ecosys­tem he says the field needs.

shelf.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Reforms in India: 10 Years After the IBC (forthcoming book, 2026)
shelf.why: A live at­tempt to bring re­searchers back to­gether on bank­ruptcy after the com­mu­nity scat­tered.

shelf.title: An annotated reading list on the Indian bankruptcy reform (2018)
shelf.creator: The Leap Journal blog
shelf.why: A guided route into the lit­er­a­ture for any­one who wants to go deeper than this episode.

shelf.title: State-of-the-art reviews of the Indian bankruptcy reform (2016, 2017, 2018)
shelf.creator: The Leap Journal blog
shelf.why: Year-by-year snap­shots of how the re­form was pro­gress­ing: the kind of on­go­ing pub­lic crit­i­cism Ajay says keeps pol­i­cy­mak­ers hon­est.

shelf.title: Code 2.0
shelf.creator: Lawrence Lessig
shelf.why: The first book he thinks of on the power of law and how every word mat­ters.

shelf.title: Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid
shelf.creator: George Roy Hill
shelf.why: A light pick after an hour on banks and cred­i­tors.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Ep 21, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Ep 34, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Ep 37, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How Indian firms moved from re­gional satraps in the 1980s to top-down ‘imperial’ firms with uni­form best prac­tices, and then to ‘adaptive’ firms that pair rules with local flex­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Ep 48, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Ep 41, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: The Nature of the Firm
shelf.creator: Ronald Coase
shelf.why: Coase’s an­swer to why firms exist when mar­kets can co­or­di­nate through prices: con­tract­ing is costly.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Ep 36, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: Zombie Firms and Creative Destruction (Ep 118, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A longer treat­ment of the zom­bie-firm prob­lem at the heart of this episode.

shelf.title: The Importance of Finance (Ep 125, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The very first episode Amit and Ajay recorded to­gether, on why fi­nance mat­ters.

shelf.title: The Life & Times of KP Krishnan (Ep 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, with KP Krishnan
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah Will Not Wear a Blue Tie to Work (Ep 389, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, with Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
shelf.why: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah on fi­nan­cial pri­vacy and the in­side story of how an­a­lysts and wonks came to­gether to draft India’s bank­ruptcy code, which Amit calls ab­so­lutely in­spir­ing.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Ep 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

laughs.text: Amit’s open­ing: ‘Firms are awe­some, firms are amaz­ing, firms are ed­i­fy­ing, firms are il­lu­mi­nat­ing, and when firms are sex­u­ally aroused, firms are firm.’
When Ajay casts cre­ative de­struc­tion as Vishnu and Shiva, Amit asks: ‘Am I sit­ting with Ajay Shah or am I sit­ting with my friend Devdutt Pattanaik?’

Amit on Japan: it ‘not only had zom­bie firms and zom­bie banks, she also made a lot of great zom­bie movies’. He won­ders whether to re­watch them for deeper metaphor be­yond the sur­face: ‘dead man walk­ing, axe in hand, hand chopped off.’
Ajay, on check­ing whether the Companies Act 2013 had a bank­ruptcy code: ‘I have done my fair share of bed­time read­ing of the Companies Act.’
Ajay on whether lenders keep get­ting fooled by mis­be­hav­ing pro­mot­ers: ‘The credit mar­kets in India are medium fool­ish. They are not deeply fool­ish.’

Amit wor­ries that bankers on a com­mit­tee won’t know the first thing about bis­cuits. Ajay: ‘They gave you hun­dred crore ru­pees... At that time, they’re bloody well going to un­der­stand your in­dus­try.’
Amit in­tro­duces the com­mit­tee of cred­i­tors as ‘a CoC, a cock as it were.’
On poi­son pills, Amit pic­tures ‘a rat trap in the cor­ner of­fice under the chair under the table.’ Ajay: ‘That’s lit­er­ally what can be done.’
After Ajay grades his own cre­ation a ‘C grade’ bank­ruptcy process, Amit protests that the work of Ajay, Susan and Bhargavi is ‘being dis­missed by some ran­dom uncle as third rate.’

Hindu trin­ity: Ajay maps cre­ation, preser­va­tion and de­struc­tion onto the life cycle of firms, with bank­ruptcy as Shiva’s work. ‘If you’d in­ter­fere with any one of them, the great bal­ance of the uni­verse would be dis­rupted.’
Tata Steel: Ajay’s proof that old dogs can learn new tricks. ‘Tata Steel of 2024 is un­rec­og­niz­ably dif­fer­ent from the orig­i­nal Tata Steel of Jamsetji Tata.’

SARFAESI Act, 2002: India’s first mile­stone, giv­ing se­cured cred­i­tors rights over col­lat­eral. In Ajay’s ex­am­ple, if Amit pledges ‘that pretty microphone’ and de­faults, the lender can seize it. With no forum for cred­i­tors to ne­go­ti­ate col­lec­tively, it pushed ev­ery­thing to­ward liq­ui­da­tion.
‘Turtles all the way down’: Amit’s phrase for how a law bro­ken at its foun­da­tions, in en­force­ment and state ca­pa­bil­ity, dam­ages the whole com­mer­cial cul­ture built on top of it.
